claims.text: Controlled cold deformation accelerates the onset and propagation of localized corrosion in Q235 steel under harsh chloride exposure.
Stress-relief treatment after cold deformation suppresses corrosion degradation in Q235 steel.
As-received Q235 steel has a ferrite-pearlite microstructure.
As-received Q235 steel has naturally low residual stress.
Twenty percent cold rolling introduces residual tensile stress into Q235 steel.
Twenty percent cold rolling increases the near-surface dislocation density of Q235 steel.
Annealing cold-rolled material at 400°C for one hour reduces its residual stress.
Annealing cold-rolled material at 400°C for one hour reduces its dislocation density.
Cold-deformation-induced dislocations and tensile residual stresses act as high-energy sites for anodic dissolution.
Cold-deformation-induced dislocations and tensile residual stresses promote passive-film breakdown.
Residual-stress-associated defects can act as initiation sites for pitting corrosion.
Reducing residual stress through mechanical or thermal treatment can reduce the occurrence of pitting corrosion.
Cold-rolled Q235 samples will nucleate pits faster and develop a higher pit density than untreated samples.
Cold-rolled Q235 samples will have a higher overall corrosion rate than untreated samples.
Stress-relieved cold-rolled samples will have fewer corrosion-initiation sites than cold-rolled samples without stress relief.
Stress-relieved samples will approach the corrosion behavior of untreated Q235 and exhibit a more uniform corrosion front.
The specified 400°C, one-hour stress-relief protocol will not substantially alter the alloy chemistry or gross microstructure.
A statistically significant absence of increased corrosion initiation in the cold-rolled group, or an absence of reduction after stress relief, would falsify the proposed mediator-based hypothesis.
